title: Go Right Through I Can't: Kyiv, the Photocopied Cipher, and the Machine That Asks If You Are Human
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Kyiv: The Observatory and the Reactor

stops.name: Kyiv, the birth
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing. English-language sources give 11 July 1975 (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'); some Russian-language biographical material gives 15 July. No civil birth record was located to settle the four days. The coordinate is the Kyiv city point; no hospital or address is recorded anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: Max Rafailovich Levchin is born in Kyiv, capital of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, into a family of scientists, writers and artists. The date is given as the eleventh of July in English and as the fifteenth in some Russian sources, and no register was found that would settle the four days between them. His maternal grandmother is an astrophysicist. The apartment he is carried into is Soviet, Jewish and technical, and its working currency is the kind of problem that has an answer. He will leave the country at sixteen.
suggested_refs: Soviet Kyiv, 1975: the city of his first sixteen years

stops.name: Kyiv Observatory, the grandmother's maxim
stops.date_confidence: the grandmother, her subject and the maxim are attested (archive.storied.illinois.edu/maximum-impact, which names Frima Lukatskaya as an astrophysicist at 'the Kiev Observatory' studying variable and unstable stars and quotes the maxim). WHICH observatory is not settled: the coordinate given is the Taras Shevchenko University observatory on Observatorna Street, but the Main Astronomical Observatory at Holosiiv (50.364, 30.497) is an equally good reading of 'the Kiev Observatory' and the source does not choose. The research pool's 50.458, 30.496 matched neither. The date orders the segment and is not a recorded event date.
stops.campa: Frima Lukatskaya, his mother's mother, works at the Kyiv observatory on variable and unstable stars: the ones whose light will not hold still long enough to be catalogued once and left alone. She gives her grandson a sentence he will repeat for the rest of his life. Which observatory it is remains open, the university's instrument on Observatorna Street or the larger installation out at Holosiiv, and the account that preserves the maxim does not say. Forty years later he will endow a scholarship in her name at a university on another continent.
stops.quote_source: Frima Lukatskaya to her grandson, quoted in STORIED, University of Illinois
suggested_refs: The Astronomical Observatory of Taras Shevchenko National University, Observatorna Street, Kyiv
The Main Astronomical Observatory at Holosiiv, the competing reading

stops.name: Kyiv, Zoryaniy Shlyah and the fan club
stops.date_confidence: the club and his father's membership are attested in Levchin's own blog post on Shamir secret sharing (max.levch.in, 2023, fetched directly). The date is an ordering device inside his childhood; the post gives no year for the membership and no meeting address is recorded.
stops.campa: His father is an active member of Zoryaniy Shlyah, a science-fiction club, in a state that pays attention to what people read together. The club is a social technology before it is a literary one: translated paperbacks moving hand to hand, names in other cities, favors owed and repaid outside the official channels for owing and repaying. Levchin will later name this network, not the money and not the paperwork, as the thing his family actually carried out of the Soviet Union.
stops.quote: My dad was a highly active member of Zoryaniy Shlyah - Kyiv's possibly first (and possibly only, at the time) sci-fi fan club
stops.quote_source: Max Levchin, blog post on Shamir secret sharing, max.levch.in (2023)
suggested_refs: Zoryaniy Shlyah, the Kyiv science-fiction fan club of the 1980s

stops.name: Kyiv, the reactor to the north
stops.date_confidence: the Chernobyl disaster is attested to 26 April 1986. Levchin's account of his family's response, the early private warning and the decision to send the two boys south, is [R]: it comes only from his own retrospective interviews, and no document places the family's movements in those weeks.
stops.campa: The reactor at Chernobyl explodes about eighty miles north. Kyiv is not told, and the parade for May Day goes ahead in the open air. Levchin's parents learn what has happened before any announcement, and they put him and his younger brother Sergey on a train south, out from under the plume. He is ten. The information reaches them privately, ahead of the state, and they act on it the same day. The whole of this account is his own, given in interviews decades later, and no document follows the family through those weeks.
suggested_refs: The Chernobyl disaster of 26 April 1986 and the delayed evacuation of Kyiv
sources: Levchin's retrospective accounts as reported in biographical profiles [R]

stops.name: Simferopol, the Geiger counter
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout, from Levchin's own recollection. The Crimean destination is NOT established in any source consulted; Simferopol is used as the rail gateway to the peninsula, which is an inference about a route rather than a claim about a town. The May date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The brothers come off the train into Crimea and are met with a Geiger counter, an instrument held against a child to find out how much of a reactor he is carrying. What it read is not recorded. Which town in Crimea received them is not recorded either, in anything reachable; the peninsula is simply where Soviet families are sent to be made well, sanatoria and grape arbors and the Black Sea. In the spring of 1986 it is also, and only, somewhere the wind was not going.
suggested_refs: Crimea in 1986, destination of children evacuated from Kyiv after Chernobyl
sources: Levchin's retrospective accounts as reported in biographical profiles [R]

stops.name: Kyiv, falling in love with secret codes
stops.date_confidence: attested in Levchin's own words (max.levch.in, 2023, fetched directly), which date it to about a year before the family left Ukraine. The family left in mid-1991, so 1990 is his own arithmetic and the month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: About a year before the family leaves, Levchin falls in love with cryptography. There is nearly nothing to read. The Soviet Union does not carry the open Western literature, and the American standard he will study four years later is not to be had in Kyiv at any price. What he has instead are puzzles, substitution ciphers, and one idea large enough to hold a career: that a message can be built to survive being intercepted by the people it was not written for. He dates the beginning of it himself, to about a year before the family left.
stops.quote: I had fallen desperately in love with secret codes and cryptography about a year before we left Ukraine.
stops.quote_source: Max Levchin, blog post on Shamir secret sharing, max.levch.in (2023)
suggested_refs: Cryptography as a closed subject in the late Soviet Union

segments.name: Out on One of the Last Pan Am Routes

stops.name: Sheremetyevo, Moscow: the flight out
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Pan Am detail and the July departure rest entirely on Levchin's own retrospective telling; the Illinois-published account says only that the family emigrated in 1991, with no date and no airline. Sheremetyevo specifically is an inference from 'flew from Moscow' and is not stated in any source fetched. Pan Am ceased operations in December 1991, so the timing is at least consistent.
stops.campa: The family flies out of Moscow as refugees on one of the last routes Pan Am is still flying; the airline itself will be gone by December. Five of them, a few hundred dollars, and whatever an emigrating Soviet family is permitted to carry through a customs hall. Levchin has repeated the Pan Am detail for thirty years and no ticket, manifest or record confirms it. Which airport in Moscow is a guess made here and marked as one. Six weeks after they land, the coup in Moscow fails and the Union begins coming apart behind them.
suggested_refs: Pan American World Airways' final Soviet routes, 1991
sources: Levchin's own dating as reported in biographical profiles [R]

stops.name: O'Hare, Chicago: the arrival
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 16 July 1991 arrival date is Levchin's own, repeated in interviews and unconfirmed by any document. O'Hare is an inference from 'moved to Chicago' and is named in no fetched source. The arrival sum is genuinely inconsistent across his own tellings and is left unresolved in the prose.
stops.campa: They land in the United States on the sixteenth of July, by his own reckoning. Levchin is sixteen, speaks little English, and has moved in one flight from a country with no private property to one where everything his family owns fits inside an envelope. What is in the envelope changes from telling to telling: six hundred dollars, seven hundred, three hundred something among five of us. None of the figures is large and none of them is documented anywhere but in his own accounts.
stops.quote: In the summer of 1991, my family and I moved to Chicago from Kyiv, Ukraine. While we had just a few hundred dollars between the five of us, we did have one secret advantage: science fiction fans.
stops.quote_source: Max Levchin, blog post on Shamir secret sharing, max.levch.in (2023)
suggested_refs: Soviet Jewish refugee arrivals in the United States, 1991
sources: Levchin's own dating in profile interviews [R]

stops.name: Rogers Park, Chicago: the household set down
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia confirms only that the family settled in Chicago in 1991. The neighborhood comes from the Illinois-published account (archive.storied.illinois.edu/maximum-impact), which names Rogers Park; the research pool carried a West Ridge coordinate with no source, and this file follows the named source instead. The September date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Levchins settle in Rogers Park, at the top edge of the city, where relatives already are. Max enters an American school with almost no English and the reading habits of a boy raised on a physicist's shelf. The neighborhood is one of the places Chicago has always put arriving families: three-flats, a lake at the end of the street, six languages on one block. Wikipedia, which is the only encyclopedic source on him, says Chicago and stops there. The neighborhood comes from his own university's magazine.
suggested_refs: Rogers Park, Chicago, and the Soviet Jewish emigration of the early 1990s

stops.name: Chicago, the cheapest machine on the floor
stops.date_confidence: [R], from a Washington Post interview paraphrased in the research dossier and not independently fetched. The store is not identified in any account; the coordinate is a downtown-Chicago placeholder and marks the city, not a shop. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He reads Computer Shopper the way other boys read a catalogue of cars, picks out a specific machine, and asks his mother to spend most of what the family has on it. A relative is sent to make the purchase and comes back with the cheapest computer on the floor at a CompUSA. Levchin has told this story for decades without softening it. He wanted a particular machine badly enough to learn everything about it, and then he got a worse one and learned everything about that.
suggested_refs: Computer Shopper magazine, the 1990s mail-order catalogue of the American PC
sources: Washington Post interview material as paraphrased in the research dossier [R]

stops.name: Mather High School, the computer club
stops.date_confidence: the school is attested (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin' and Wikipedia, 'Stephen Tyng Mather High School'); the friendship with Erik Klein and his later role at PayPal are dossier detail, [R]. The September date orders the segment; his years of attendance are not precisely recorded.
stops.campa: At Stephen Tyng Mather High School on North Lincoln Avenue he joins the computer club, which is where a boy with no English and a bad machine can be understood without translation. There he becomes close to Erik Klein. Nearly a decade later, when Levchin needs engineers he can trust inside a company hemorrhaging money to fraud, Klein is one of the people he calls, and the friendship outlasts the company. The club has one machine that everybody uses and an argument about how it works that runs longer than the meetings do.
suggested_refs: Stephen Tyng Mather High School, 5835 N. Lincoln Avenue, Chicago
sources: dossier detail for the Klein friendship [R]

stops.name: University of Illinois, the xeroxed cipher
stops.date_confidence: the 1994 date and the whole episode are attested in Levchin's own words (LinkedIn Pulse). Note that the commonly cited 1993 enrollment year is NOT in the Wikipedia article usually credited with it, which states only the 1997 degree; it is a back-computation from a four-year course and is not asserted here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A fellow student lends him a many-times-photocopied copy of the United States government specification for the Digital Encryption Standard. It is 1994. The document is a public federal standard, printed and freely distributable, and it reaches him the way contraband reaches anyone: as a bad xerox, passed hand to hand, letters filling in from the toner of the copy before. He reads it. Four years earlier, in Kyiv, no version of this paper existed to be had at any price, and everything he knew about ciphers he had worked out from puzzles.
stops.quote: I loved math and puzzles for as long as I can remember, but my love affair with cryptography began when a fellow student at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign let me borrow his many-times-xerox'd copy of the government-issued technical specification of the Digital Encryption Standard in 1994.
stops.quote_source: Max Levchin, 'Why I Created the First Prize for Real-World Cryptography,' LinkedIn Pulse
suggested_refs: FIPS 46, the Data Encryption Standard, and its circulation among American undergraduates
sources: Max Levchin, 'Why I Created the First Prize for Real-World Cryptography,' LinkedIn Pulse

stops.name: Champaign, SponsorNet New Media
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1995 (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'); the composition of the founding group is dossier detail. Day defaulted. No company records were located.
stops.campa: Still an undergraduate, Levchin co-founds SponsorNet New Media with Luke Nosek and Scott Banister, selling advertising on a web that has only just worked out it can be sold on. It does not become anything. Almost nothing survives of it in the record except the roster, and the roster turns out to be the point: two of the three will be in Palo Alto with him within four years, building the company that matters. He is nineteen and has started the first of a sequence he later describes as shots on goal.
suggested_refs: SponsorNet New Media, 1995, one of the first campus web-advertising ventures
sources: research dossier for the founding roster [R]

stops.name: Champaign, NetMeridian Software
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The January 1996 to December 1998 span and the CEO title are reported from PayPal's SEC biography as summarized in dossier material, and were not re-verified against filing text in this pass. No products are documented anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: He founds NetMeridian Software and runs it as chief executive, writing security applications for the internet and for palmtop computers, the small handheld machines that are briefly and confidently the future. It is precisely the work he will do next: encryption on a device that fits in a pocket and is easily left in a taxi. PayPal's own filings will carry this line in his biography years later, which is very nearly the only place it survives. What NetMeridian actually shipped is not documented in any source that could be located.
suggested_refs: Palmtop and PalmPilot security software, 1996-1998
sources: PayPal SEC biography as summarized in the research dossier [R]

stops.name: University of Illinois, the degree and the failure after it
stops.date_confidence: the 1997 B.S. in computer science is attested (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'); the May date is the conventional commencement month and is an ordering device. The post-graduation venture that failed, and the August 1998 move west, are [R] from profile material.
stops.campa: He takes the bachelor's degree in computer science six years after arriving in the country with no English and a few hundred dollars. He does not leave for California immediately. One more venture started near the university fails first, and by his own account it is the failure rather than the diploma that moves him: what Illinois cannot supply is the density of other people trying the same thing at the same hour. Champaign has the machines, the library and the cohort, and it does not have the market. In August of the following year he goes west.
suggested_refs: The University of Illinois computer science cohort of the mid-1990s
sources: profile material for the failed venture [R]

stops.name: Palo Alto, the move west
stops.date_confidence: [R]. August 1998 is widely repeated in profiles and carried by Wikipedia, but is not independently corroborated. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from peter_thiel.journey.json, stop 'Palo Alto, Thiel Capital and the founding of Confinity'. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He arrives in Palo Alto at twenty-three with a failed venture behind him and the Illinois cohort scattering toward the same few streets. The move is the entire strategy. The industry he wants is not distributed across a country; it is concentrated in the space between a university and a downtown, and it hires by proximity and introduction. Within four months he has met Peter Thiel, who is running a small fund out of the same blocks, and the two of them have a company for putting encrypted money on handheld computers.
suggested_refs: University Avenue, Palo Alto, 1998

stops.name: Palo Alto, Confinity incorporated
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1998 with NO day. PayPal's final prospectus (424B4, 15 February 2002) says only 'Confinity, Inc., a development stage company, incorporated in California in December 1998,' and the management biographies repeat 'in December 1998'. The research pool's '3 December' has no source and is not used. Note California, not Delaware. No street address for the first office is established in any filing; coordinate inherited byte-identical from peter_thiel.journey.json.
stops.campa: Confinity, Inc. is incorporated in California in December, first under the working name Fieldlink. Levchin is chief technology officer and a director. Peter Thiel puts in about a hundred thousand dollars out of a fund he raised from family and friends; Luke Nosek comes from Illinois. The product beams encrypted money between PalmPilots, and it turns out that almost nobody wants to beam money between PalmPilots. The thing that works is the demonstration built to move money by email, written as an afterthought, and it is called PayPal.
suggested_refs: PayPal, Inc., Form 424B4, 15 February 2002, on Confinity's California incorporation

stops.name: Stanford, the cryptographers a mile away
stops.date_confidence: [R] and flagged as needing verification. The claim that Dan Boneh advised Confinity's handheld security design and that Martin Hellman advised and invested comes from the research dossier only; no Boneh or Hellman interview was fetched in this pass. The date orders the segment. If the claim fails, the stop should go.
stops.campa: Two Stanford cryptographers are reported to work on the young company's problems: Dan Boneh on the handheld security design, and Martin Hellman, who published the first public key exchange in 1976, as adviser and investor. Levchin's line to the founders of modern cryptography is usually drawn honorifically, through a prize he has not yet endowed. What is claimed here is plainer than that: two men on a campus a mile from the office who take his calls. No source confirming either role could be located, and the claim is recorded as unverified rather than told as a scene.
suggested_refs: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography' (1976)
An interview or filing that would confirm the Boneh and Hellman roles at Confinity: not located

stops.name: Palo Alto, X.com merges with Confinity
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly. PayPal's 424B4 (2002-02-15): 'On March 30, 2000, X.com merged with Confinity.' X.com Corporation was the legal survivor and the renaming came later. The research pool's '1-30 March 2000' range collapses to this one date. The 46.5 percent figure and the shared-building claim are dossier-only [R]. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from elon_musk.journey.json, stop 'X.com, Palo Alto'.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of March, X.com merges with Confinity. Elon Musk's company is the legal survivor; Confinity's holders take a little under half of what results. The two firms have been racing the same product from the same street and buying users off each other with referral bonuses, at a burn rate neither can hold. Inside the merged company the first fight is technical. Musk wants the stack on Windows, and Levchin's engineers want Unix, and neither side treats the question as a question about servers.
suggested_refs: PayPal, Inc., Form 424B4, 15 February 2002, on the merger of 30 March 2000

stops.name: Palo Alto, the test that asks if you are human
stops.date_confidence: [R], tag deliberately lowered. The Gausebeck-Levchin test is documented only through later retrospectives, including Sequoia's 'Crucible Moments: PayPal' oral history. Neither the name Gausebeck nor any description of a distorted-text test appears anywhere in PayPal's final prospectus, which was searched in full. The 2000 date has no primary support and the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Fraud is eating the company at a rate that can kill it: accounts opened in bulk by programs, stolen cards, losses running ahead of revenue on a service designed to move money instantly and irreversibly. Levchin and an engineer named David Gausebeck put distorted text on the screen and require the applicant to type it back, on the reasoning that a human eye reads what a program of 2000 cannot. It is among the first such systems run at commercial scale. He is twenty-five. When exactly it went up nobody recorded: the prospectus filed two years later, searched in full, never mentions Gausebeck or the test at all.
suggested_refs: The Gausebeck-Levchin test and the early history of CAPTCHA
Sequoia Capital, 'Crucible Moments: PayPal' oral history, with Levchin and Dave Gausebeck

stops.name: Palo Alto, the board acts during a honeymoon
stops.date_confidence: the September 2000 board removal of Musk and the installation of Thiel are attested and are recorded identically in elon_musk.journey.json and peter_thiel.journey.json, from which this coordinate is inherited byte-identical. Levchin's presence at the board action is stated in NO source; his role as CTO and director at the time is separately attested, so his proximity is inferred here and not asserted. That he opposed Musk's technical direction is [R], from company oral histories. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: While Musk is abroad on his honeymoon the board removes him as chief executive and puts Peter Thiel in the seat. The operating-system question and the product question both settle the way Levchin's engineers wanted them settled. No account places him in the room, names him among those who moved, or records what he said; he was the company's chief technology officer and a director, and that is the whole of what the record will support. The company drops the letter X from the door and calls itself PayPal.
suggested_refs: The September 2000 board action replacing Musk with Thiel

stops.name: Nasdaq MarketSite, New York: thirteen dollars a share
stops.date_confidence: two dates split. The offering priced at $13.00 on the evening of 14 February 2002; the final prospectus was filed 15 February and trading opened that day under PYPL, which is the date used. Share counts from the 424B4. Trading is electronic and no source places Levchin at the MarketSite in person; the coordinate is the conventional landmark, inherited byte-identical from peter_thiel.journey.json.
stops.campa: PayPal prices at thirteen dollars a share on the evening of the fourteenth and opens the next morning under the ticker PYPL: five million four hundred thousand shares, with an over-allotment of eight hundred and ten thousand behind them. It is one of very few technology listings to get out alive in the two years after the crash. Levchin is chief technology officer and a director, holding 1,738,167 shares, which the prospectus puts at 3.2 percent of the company. He is twenty-six.
suggested_refs: PayPal, Inc., Form 424B4, 15 February 2002: offering terms and beneficial ownership

stops.name: eBay headquarters, San Jose: the sale closes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 October 2002 at $1.5 billion in eBay stock (Wikipedia, 'PayPal'). A contradiction is deliberately left open, as it is in peter_thiel.journey.json: Wikipedia's 'eBay' article gives $1.4 billion at closing against $1.5 billion announced. Levchin's proceeds, roughly $34 million on about 2.3 percent per Wikipedia, do not reconcile with the prospectus, which gives him 2.9 percent after the offering. The 2007 magazine photo spread usually credited with coining 'PayPal Mafia' could not be located in this pass, so the naming of the group is [R]. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from peter_thiel.journey.json.
stops.campa: eBay closes its all-stock purchase of the company that had been feeding on eBay's own auctions. The announced value is one and a half billion dollars. Levchin's stake pays out at something near thirty-four million by the figure most often repeated, though the percentage attached to it in those accounts does not match the one his own prospectus printed eight months earlier, and nobody has reconciled them. Within a decade the business press will have a name for the group that scatters out of the building, borrowed from organized crime. Nobody has produced the 2007 magazine spread usually credited with coining it.
suggested_refs: The eBay acquisition of PayPal, announced July 2002, closed 3 October 2002

stops.name: PayPal headquarters, North First Street, San Jose: the CTO leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 2002 (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'); day defaulted. The description of the aftermath as psychologically difficult is [R], his own language in later interviews. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from elon_musk.journey.json. The TR100 listing is attested to 2002.
stops.campa: He stays to the end of the year as chief technology officer of what is now a division of eBay, and then he goes. He is twenty-seven and rich, and he has spent four years inside a fight that never once paused: fraud, the merger, the board, the market, the sale. In later interviews he describes what followed as psychologically hard, which is not the customary register for a man who has just been paid. The same year MIT Technology Review puts him on its list of the hundred best innovators under thirty-five.
suggested_refs: MIT Technology Review TR100, 2002

segments.name: San Francisco: The Check, the Slideshow, the Search Company

stops.name: San Francisco, the million-dollar check
stops.date_confidence: the $1 million angel investment through MRL Ventures in Stoppelman and Simmons is attested (Wikipedia, 'Yelp'). The 29th-birthday-lunch framing is Levchin's own [R], and the Slanted Door as its venue appears in NO source fetched: Wikipedia's Yelp article does not mention the lunch at all, so no restaurant is staged here. July is his birth month and orders the stop.
stops.campa: Through MRL Ventures, his own small vehicle, Levchin puts a million dollars into a local-recommendation service two Illinois associates want to build, Jeremy Stoppelman and Russel Simmons. He will chair its board for about a decade. He tells the founding as a birthday lunch: twenty-nine years old, an idea across the table, a check afterward. The corporate record confirms the vehicle and confirms the million dollars, and says nothing whatever about a lunch.
suggested_refs: MRL Ventures and the 2004 angel round in Yelp
sources: Levchin's own founder narrative in profile interviews [R]

stops.name: San Francisco, Slide
stops.date_confidence: January 2005, corrected from the research pool's 2004. Two SEC proxy statements Levchin reviewed as a director state it identically: Yahoo! DEF 14A (2013-04-30) and Yelp DEF 14A (2015-04-10), 'founder and Chief Executive Officer of Slide, Inc. ... from January 2005 to August 2010, when it was acquired by Google.' Wikipedia's 'Slide (website)' page returned 404. The office coordinate is approximate.
stops.campa: Levchin founds Slide: slideshows first, then widgets, then social games, running inside MySpace and later Facebook. He is founder and chief executive. It is the opposite of PayPal in every dimension he cares about, consumer instead of financial, decorative instead of adversarial, and above all built on distribution he does not own. Two proxy statements he later signs off on as a director date the founding to January 2005. Wikipedia's page on the company returns a 404.
suggested_refs: Yahoo! Inc., DEF 14A (30 April 2013) and Yelp Inc., DEF 14A (10 April 2015), for the January 2005 founding date

stops.name: Googleplex, Mountain View: Slide acquired
stops.date_confidence: the August 2010 acquisition and the vice-presidency are attested (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'); the reported $182 million price is dossier detail not independently re-verified. Day defaulted. The coordinate is the Googleplex, the company's headquarters, not a confirmed office of Levchin's.
stops.campa: Google buys Slide, reportedly for a hundred and eighty-two million dollars, and Levchin becomes a vice president of engineering. The company doing the buying is losing the social question badly and knows it, and the company being bought is a social-games business with a team Google wants more than it wants the games. He arrives at Mountain View with his engineers and a mandate to fix something enormous. He is thirty-five and has not had a manager since he was an undergraduate.
suggested_refs: The Google acquisition of Slide, August 2010

stops.name: Googleplex, Mountain View: Slide shut down
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 August 2011 for the closure and Levchin's departure (Wikipedia, 'Max Levchin'). Same coordinate as the acquisition stop.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of August, a year after buying it, Google shuts Slide down, kills most of its products, and Levchin leaves the same day. The purchase had bought a team rather than a business, and the team is redistributed into the search company like water into a reservoir. He has now sold one company into an acquirer that renamed it and one into an acquirer that closed it. He is thirty-six, and he will not build on ground he does not own again.
suggested_refs: The closure of Slide, 26 August 2011

stops.name: San Francisco, HVF opens
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing. Wikipedia dates the founding to late 2011, which is the date used; both the Yahoo! DEF 14A (2013-04-30) and the Yelp DEF 14A (2015-04-10) say instead 'Since January 2012, Mr. Levchin has been Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of HVF, LLC, a start-up lab focused on extracting insights from recordable information.' The prose uses the SEC's description of the thesis, which differs from the dossier's framing. No street address is established; coordinate approximate.
stops.campa: He starts HVF, for Hard, Valuable, Fun: a laboratory and studio rather than a company, built to start several things at once from one thesis, that recorded information is being generated far faster than anyone is extracting value from it. There is no product and no customer. There is a room, and in it a proposition and a founder who does not need the money. Two companies come out of it. One lends and one measures fertility, and both of them ask what a body of recorded data will say about the person who produced it.
suggested_refs: Yahoo! Inc., DEF 14A (30 April 2013), describing HVF, LLC as a start-up lab

stops.name: 650 California Street, San Francisco: Affirm
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2012 for the founding, with Nathan Gettings, Jeffrey Kaditz and Alex Rampell, at 650 California Street (Wikipedia, 'Affirm (company)'). Month and day defaulted; no founding day is recorded.
stops.campa: Affirm is founded out of HVF by Levchin with Nathan Gettings, Jeffrey Kaditz and Alex Rampell. Levchin spent four years at PayPal learning exactly how much a stranger's transaction can be made to reveal, and the new company is that knowledge turned around and pointed the other way.
